summary: Give each client a fair request budget so one runaway script cannot crowd out everyone.
goals: How one client can use shared capacity
How token buckets and other limits work
How gateways share a client’s limit
How 429 responses and tenant quotas help
How to drop low-priority work during overload

steps.title: One client can use all the capacity
body: A customer’s script has a bug and calls your API in a tight loop: 5,000 requests every second. The API servers spend nearly all their time on this script. Real users wait behind it and time out. Nobody attacked the service; one client is simply using more than its share.
steps.callout: Shared capacity needs a fairness rule. Without one, the loudest client can use it all.

steps.title: Limit requests at the front door
body: Put a rate limiter in the gateway before the API. Identify each client by API key, user ID, or IP address, and give it a budget such as 10 requests per second. Allow requests within the budget. Reject extra requests right away with 429 Too Many Requests, before they use API resources.
steps.callout: An early rejection is cheap: the gateway answers in microseconds, and the API never handles the extra request.

steps.title: Use a token bucket
body: A common method is the token bucket. Each client has a bucket that holds up to 10 tokens. The bucket refills at 10 tokens per second. Each request uses one token; if none remain, the gateway returns 429. A real user’s bucket may stay mostly full, while a fast script empties its bucket and gets limited.
steps.callout: The bucket size allows a short burst. The refill rate limits the average over time.

steps.title: Compare counting methods
body: A fixed window counts requests in each calendar minute and resets at :00. A client can use its full budget at 12:00:59, then use it again at 12:01:00—twice the limit in two seconds. A sliding window smooths that boundary. A token bucket allows a controlled burst. Many API gateways use a sliding window or token bucket.
steps.callout: If you need a steady outflow to a fragile partner API, a leaky bucket can queue requests and release them at a fixed pace.

steps.title: Share one limit across gateways
body: A service may need several gateways. If each keeps a separate counter, a client spread across 10 gateways could get 10 times its limit. Keep the counter in a shared fast store such as Redis. Each gateway atomically increases the counter and checks the total.
steps.callout: A shared store adds about 1 ms per request. Some systems trade exact counts for speed by syncing local counters once a second.

steps.title: Tell clients when to try again
body: A useful 429 response tells the client when to return. Include a Retry-After: 30 header and headers showing the limit and remaining requests. A well-behaved client waits before retrying. The script owner can fix the loop so it uses its fair share.
steps.callout: Publish limits in the API documentation. Offer higher limits to customers who need them.

steps.title: Limit traffic per customer too
body: One company uses your API through 10,000 users for a nightly import. Each person stays within their own limit, but together they use 70% of your capacity. Other customers slow down. A per-user limit cannot catch this. Add a limit for each tenant (customer account), based on its plan, as well as per-user limits.
steps.callout: Limits can be layered by user, customer, endpoint, and the whole system. Expensive endpoints can have lower limits.

steps.title: Drop low-priority work first
body: Rate limits stop one client from using too much capacity. On launch day, all users may arrive at once and total demand can still exceed what the system serves. Load shedding means deliberately dropping lower-priority requests first. The gateway can reject background work such as prefetching, recommendations, and analytics so logins and checkouts continue working.
steps.callout: Failing some requests on purpose can be better than letting every request fail by accident.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Give each client a budget and reject excess requests early with 429.
  • A token bucket allows short bursts but limits the average rate.
  • Use a shared store to coordinate limits across gateways.
  • Set limits per user, customer, endpoint, and system.
  • During overload, shed low-priority work first.
